Question: If atheism is true, why are there still monkeys? I thought monkeys evolved into humans over billions of years.
Old_Answer: The broad pattern of evolution is diversification to take advantage of new and varied ecological niches. Just for a moment, consider birds, and how many different species of birds there are today. You probably wouldn’t ask why other birds are still around if golden eagles evolved from birds. It hopefully seems obvious that golden eagles aren’t the only successful lifestyle for birds, and that there are lots of other ways for other bird species to survive without becoming more like golden eagles. In fact, it’s downright advantageous. There are only so many resources to go around in the golden eagle niche, so it’s better for other bird species to find other ways to make a living to have access to different resources. A hummingbird doesn’t have to compete with a golden eagle for food, while penguins can survive in environments that would kill eagles. It’s the same way with so many other branches of life, from beetles to ants to rodents to us monkeys. Successful lineages branch out and become more diverse, as they split up into more and more species to take advantage of more opportunities. Here’s a high level family tree of primates: ABOVE SOURCE: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960982212008068 Now sure, you can play semantic games over whether those ‘Early simians’ should be called monkeys or not, but I think if we had a time machine and could bring one to the present, most people would think of it as a monkey. And monkeys have been a successful enough lineage that modern day monkeys have diversified into hundreds of species, from New World monkeys to Old World monkeys to apes, and yes, that includes us humans, as well. In other words, there are still other monkeys besides people because monkeys are a successful lineage, and there are lots of niches that they’ve evolved to take advantage of. Just to clarify, from those earliest monkeys to us humans has only taken tens of millions of years, not billions. And I know there are also more semantics around whether apes are monkeys or not, but I’ve come around to the idea that ‘monkey’ should be a monophyletic group, and that us apes should just be considered as a branch of monkeys.

This means that both humans and monkeys have evolved along separate paths from that shared ancestor. Question: Where does the concept of the Earth being six thousand years old come from? Is it from the Bible?
Old_Answer: It really does come from the Bible, if a bit indirectly. There are several passages in the Bible that give information on such things as how old people were when they had children or how long certain periods lasted, that if accepted at face value, can give a very close approximation of when Adam and Eve were created (according to the stories, at least). There are a few places where things get somewhat murky, but not enough to change things by more than a few decades* – nothing on the order of millions or billions of years. This was a fairly well accepted interpretation for generations, and many scholars made their own estimates of when creation would have taken place, including Johannes Kepler. Arguably the most respected of these was the estimate done by James Ussher, who put much effort into sorting out the murky periods. It's because Ussher's chronology was so well respected that it was included in the introductory material to several printed Bibles, including the famed Scofield Bible. Wikipedia gives a good summary of how Ussher made his estimate (Ussher chronology - Wikipedia). He broke it down into three periods: Using other sources outside the Bible, Ussher determined the enthronement of the Babylonian king Amel-Marduk to have occurred in 562 BC, which was tied in to the end of the Babylonian Captivity through 2 Kings 25:27. From there, it was just a matter of going backwards by all the years previously calculated, putting creation at 4004 BC. Creation to Exodus You can easily look up Genesis 5 and Genesis 11 for yourself, but to give an idea, here's the start of Genesis 5: This is the list of the descendants of Adam. When God created humans,[a] he made them[b] in the likeness of God. 2 Male and female he created them, and he blessed them and called them humans[c] when they were created. 3 When Adam had lived one hundred thirty years, he became the father of a son in his likeness, according to his image, and named him Seth. 4 The days of Adam after he became the father of Seth were eight hundred years, and he had other sons and daughters. 5 Thus all the days that Adam lived were nine hundred thirty years, and he died. 6 When Seth had lived one hundred five years, he became the father of Enosh. 7 Seth lived after the birth of Enosh eight hundred seven years and had other sons and daughters. 8 Thus all the days of Seth were nine hundred twelve years, and he died. It goes on and on like that. So, as long as you accept these statements as true, it's mostly a simple matter of adding up how old each man was when he begat his heir. The only real hiccups are between Noah and Shem, and between Nahor and Terah. Both of these are somewhat ambiguous. In the former, the passage states, "After Noah was five hundred years old, Noah became the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth." In the latter, the passage is, "When Terah had lived seventy years, he became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran." People who care about this issue more than I do have gone into detail to try to pinpoint those ages (e.g. Contradictions: Noah’s Three Sons). You also need to know how old Abraham was when the Exodus occurred. His age at the start of all those events comes from Genesis 12:4, "So Abram went, as the Lord had told him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran." I ran the math myself with a spreadsheet, and came up with 2049 years from the creation of Adam to the birth of Abraham, plus another 75 years until the Exodus, for 2124 years total (a bit different from Ussher because I didn't put in the effort to figure out the ambiguity around Noah/Shem and Nahor/Terah). I suppose there's one other hiccup, depending on which particular version of the Bible you're using. Since we don't have an 'original' version of Genesis, we have to rely on copies of that version, most notably the Masoretic text and the Septuagint (though those aren't the only two). And those copies differ on certain details, including all those ages in Genesis 5 and Genesis 11. Exodus to Solomon's Temple Like I said, this one comes straight from a single verse, 1 Kings 6:1: In the four hundred eightieth year after the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv, which is the second month, he began to build the house of the Lord. Solomon's Temple to the Babylonian Captivity This is the period where things purportedly get a bit more complicated. I haven't gone through this period in detail, yet, myself, but to give just one example, you have this verse from 2 Kings 3:1: In the eighteenth year of King Jehoshaphat of Judah, Jehoram son of Ahab became king over Israel in Samaria; he reigned twelve years. Go through finding all those verses and work out the years, and you come up a little over 4 centuries of history. In a somewhat independent path, other books in the Bible also give more genealogies, such that you can trace each and every claimed descendant from Adam all the way to Jesus. Granted, there aren't ages associated with all of those genealogies, but these also give a ballpark range in the thousands of years. So, if you accept the claims of the Bible at more or less face value, and assume all those genealogies represent real people and not just imaginary people made up out of thin air, and that all the events in Egypt, Israel, and Judah all really happened, you'll end up at an estimate for the date of creation somewhere around 4000 BC. As a side note, while it seems to be somewhat fashionable to dismiss exercises like these because some parts of the Bible were ‘obviously’ meant to be taken more metaphorically or allegorically, I don’t see such figurative interpretations as obvious at all. The crux of this argument would be the genealogies in Genesis 5 and Genesis 11 – after that, you’re already into Egyptian pharaohs, so nothing that’s going to be a major difference from real history (at least as far as timelines). But these genealogies aren’t fables with moral lessons or some type of simplified explanation of complex concepts for a pre-scientific society. They’re boring, dry lists of ancestry. It’s about as close to a conventional history section as you’ll find in Genesis – the part least likely to be metaphorical or allegorical (though there’s certainly a reason to ‘invent’ such lists to provide legitimacy for the rulers of Israel and Judah). *As I already touched upon, that difference of only a few decades is using a specific version of the Bible, such as the Masoretic text or the Septuagint. The differences between those different versions can add up to a couple millennia, though still not anywhere near on the magnitude of real history.

Question: ‘After-birth abortion’: Are they serious?
Old_Answer: Well, if you look at the actual situations where this is being discussed rather than just fear mongering about imaginary situations, then yes. Nobody wants to kill a healthy late term fetus or newborn. No woman goes through 9 months of pregnancy just to decide at the last minute that she's changed her mind. And certainly no doctor would kill a healthy newborn baby after the entire process of labor or a Caesarean delivery. But not all fetuses and newborns are healthy. Hopefully, with good pre-natal care, any major complications will be detected early. But not everybody has access to the best pre-natal care, and even then, some complications simply don't get detected until late into the pregnancy. And some of these complications are euphemistically referred to as "incompatible with life". In other words, they're complications so severe that the baby won't survive even with the best medical treatment available. Trying to treat these conditions will only delay the inevitable and prolong the suffering. So, the question becomes, what truly is the most humane and merciful course of action in these cases? Prolonging suffering, or doing what you can to ease the pain and try to end the suffering as soon as possible? In another recent answer, Jeff Lewis's answer to Democrats support post-birth abortion, but isn’t abortion after birth just murder?, I discussed a study that polled "physicians and paramedical professionals involved in late TOP [termination of pregnancy] decision‐making in all eight centers with a Neonatal Intensive Care Unit in Flanders, Belgium (N = 117)". As I pointed out in that answer, "These aren't folks for whom this question is a mere hypothetical. They have to see the consequences and suffering of the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit on a daily basis." And such health care professionals were overwhelmingly in favor of "actively terminat[ing] life" for newborns with serious enough conditions. And while the support for feticide wasn't quite so overwhelming, a majority still supported feticide over palliative care in serious enough cases. So yes, sometimes the humane and merciful choice is to end a poor newborn's suffering. It's a tragedy, and would be absolutely gut wrenching to the parents (and the doctors – they're humans, too). But the alternative is just forcing the newborn to suffer longer before still eventually dying. Seriously, these are profound and extremely serious situations that some families find themselves in. Let's not take away the merciful options in an already shitty situation just so we can shout some slogans to win political points. ETA: After some feedback in the comments, I want to be very clear on this. I'm talking about newborns with severe complications and no chance of recovery. The question is what’s best for these babies, which has to be looked at on a case by case basis. Is there any quality of life at all, or just suffering? Palliative care and hospice are already available for newborns with severe complications, ranging from not attempting to treat the condition, to withholding nutrition. And quite obviously, such infants will die. But with their condition, they would have died anyway. It certainly can't be considered more humane to prolong their suffering. And that leads into the debate raised in this question, although the OP seemed disingenuous in how they framed it, of whether active feticide is an appropriate approach for these babies, or if the current standard of palliative care is sufficient (and I really, really hope you're not against palliative care – who would actually push for making babies suffer even more). As I said in my prior answer, "I understand people's hesitancy to enable doctor's to actively end the life of patients as opposed to mere palliative care, especially in the case of patients who are too young to voice their own desires." So the question comes down to balancing the best interests of babies with such severe complications vs. how comfortable we are with intentionally taking steps to end a life. Minimizing the suffering for these babies as much as possible would require active feticide. Palliative care allows people to have an easier conscience, but forces the babies to suffer a bit longer. Active attempts to treat such conditions would prolong the suffering the longest. And as I pointed out in my answer, these aren't just hypotheticals. There are real, non-thought experiment babies suffering in NICUs right now, with parents agonizing over their decisions.

Question: What are some books that every aspiring Aerospace engineer should read?
Old_Answer: I come at this issue much more from the aero side than the space side. That said, there are a few books that I refer back to fairly often: Introduction to Flight, by John D. Anderson This is just a solid textbook on the fundamentals, with lots of interesting side notes related to aviation history. This should be the first book in your collection. You can get a good idea of the topics just from the chapter titles: 1) The First Aeronautical Engineers 2) Fundamental Thoughts 3) The Standard Atmosphere 4) Basic Aerodynamics 5) Airfoils, Wings, and Other Aerodynamics Shapes 6) Elements of Airplane Performance 7) Principles of Stability and Control 8) Space Flight (Astronautics) 9) Propulsion 10) Hypersonic Vehicles On a personal note, I'll add that Dr. Anderson is a phenomenal teacher. I had him for several of my engineering classes, as well as an honors seminar on aviation history. He gave that class a personal tour of the Air and Space Museum in D.C., which is one of the best museum visits I've ever experienced. I'll also note that my personal copy of this book is the 3rd edition, while the latest is the 9th. Aircraft Design: A Conceptual Approach, by Daniel P. Raymer Back when I was in my aircraft design class in college, we referred to this book as our Bible, both for its form factor and for the wealth of information it contained. There's just tons of practical information for designing aircraft. His empirical trends for aircraft weight estimates are a recognized standard. My copy of this book (3rd edition) has a ton of index cards and post it notes marking the sections that I refer back to the most often. Theory of Wing Sections, by Abbbott and Doenhoff This book is still the standard when it comes to airfoils. It has a large section on theory, around 250 pages worth, covering everything from simple 2D flow to 3D wings and compressibility. After that comes around 300 pages of appendices, broken down into Basic Thickness Forms, Mean Lines, Airfoil Ordinates, and finally and perhaps most usefully, Aerodynamic Characteristics, with just page after page of lift, drag, and moment curves. ABOVE: The appendix entry for the iconic NACA 0012 There are plenty of other books worth considering for your collection depending on exactly what your specialty is going to be: And more. But those three that I listed are the ones I come back to over and over. FWIW, since some of these books are classics, they're already in the public domain, so you can find online versions for free:

Question: Why do so many people hate the self checkouts?
Old_Answer: Actually, I tend to prefer it. But it really depends on the implementation, and what the store was like before they brought in the self checkouts. Let me take my local Walmart as an example. Back in the days before self checkouts, they never had enough cashiers for the number of customers. There was no such thing as a quick trip to Walmart, because you inevitably got stuck in a long line waiting to check out. Then, when they did bring in self checkouts, they brought in dozens of them. So now, there's almost always at least one self-checkout open. And even if there is a line, it's more like a bank line, where everybody waits in one line, and then just goes to the next open checkout. So it doesn't matter if there are a few folks with full carts, because they're only tying up that one particular checkout, not the entire line. Now it really is possible to be in and out of Walmart in 5 minutes if I only need one thing. I've been to other stores, though, where they've only installed a limited number of self checkouts. And the worst offenders don't even go with the bank-style lines, but have separate lines for each self checkout. Those are annoying, where you may end up waiting longer than the pre-self-checkout days. My favorite modern checkout is Sam's Club (I'd imagine the other warehouse stores have this as well, but Wichita Falls, TX doesn't give you many options). You just download an app to your phone to scan the items as you shop, swipe a button to pay with a credit card on file, and then just briefly show your phone to the receipt checker on your way out the door. It's hard to get much quicker and convenient than that. But my second favorite checkout is at a small grocery chain called United Market Street, which has a good compromise between self checkouts and old school people. They do employ plenty of real life cashiers to scan your groceries, so the lines are rarely very long. And they even still have baggers, who take your groceries out to your car for you. They also have about half a dozen self checkouts, largely to replace the express checkout. So even the express line folks don't get all that inconvenienced by somebody cheating with a cart full of 50 things. Of course, you pay for it. Their prices aren't horrible, but they're definitely higher than Walmart or Aldi. As far as a few other answers I've seen about taking away low skill jobs, meh. The recent trend of online shopping seems to have taken care of that, with employees running around to fill all those online orders. My daughter did that for a bit at the aforementioned Market Street, and I see plenty of folks with that job at my local Walmart. So, until robots take over that, those jobs offset the loss of cashiers. So as long as it's done right, and considering that stores were skimping on cashiers even before self-checkouts were a thing, I've found self-checkouts to make shopping more convenient.

For many, the primary complaint stems from the perceived loss of human interaction. Shopping has traditionally been a social experience, and the shift to self checkouts can feel impersonal. Some customers miss the friendly banter with cashiers or the simple courtesy of having someone else handle the checkout process. Additionally, there’s a significant portion of the population that finds self checkouts intimidating or confusing, particularly older individuals or those who may not be tech-savvy. The fear of making mistakes—like accidentally not scanning an item or misplacing a coupon—can lead to anxiety, making the shopping experience less enjoyable. Furthermore, there are concerns about job loss; many people feel that self checkouts contribute to the decline of cashier positions, which can be a significant source of income for many. This sentiment is compounded by the notion that stores are prioritizing profit over customer service. However, it’s worth noting that not all self checkout implementations are created equal. In some stores, they function seamlessly and enhance the shopping experience by reducing wait times. Ultimately, the backlash against self checkouts often reflects a broader discomfort with change and a longing for the familiar, coupled with practical concerns about efficiency and job security. As retailers continue to evolve, it will be interesting to see how they balance technology with the human touch that many customers still crave.

Question: How can one respond to the argument that the existence of monkeys disproves the theory of evolution?
Old_Answer: I see a lot of answers here proposing ridicule and laughter, which I think are missing a great opportunity to make somebody one of today's "lucky 10,000". ABOVE SOURCE: XKCD - Ten Thousand Anybody asking this question quite obviously didn't have the best science education growing up, so this is your chance to share the excitement of understanding a topic as enthralling as universal common descent. Anyway, as far as this particular question goes, it's been asked so many times that there are countless responses. Perhaps my favorite is to ask, if I'm descended from Germans, why are there still Germans? I think it hits on several key points in one example. First, it's obvious that I'm not descended from any living Germans. You have to go back several generations to find my most recent German ancestry. So, modern day Germans and I share a common ancestor. I'm not descended from modern day Germans. Quite literally, modern day Germans are my distant cousins, and modern day monkeys are my even more distant cousins. Related to that, the German culture of my ancestors back in Germany wasn't the same as modern day German culture. Once my family split away from our German relatives, my family's culture developed independently here in the U.S., while my cousins’ culture developed differently in Germany. Likewise, when we say that humans are descended from monkeys, those ancient species of monkeys weren't the same as modern day species of monkeys. We took one evolutionary path, and they took another. Further, this analogy shows that there's not necessarily a single ideal form that culture will develop towards, or by analogy, any single ideal form that animals will evolve towards. I'm sure American and German patriots will argue over which country is better (I actually do have very good German friends, and yes, we do argue about this good naturedly over beers), but both nations exist and are fairly successful. Looking back to the animal kingdom, there are lots of food sources, lifestyles, and niches for animals to survive in, including monkeys. Species will diversify to take advantage of all this variety of niches. There's no reason to suspect that other monkeys or apes would evolve to be more like people when they're already finding success in their own different ways. (There's also the competitive exclusion principle that predicts that no two species in the same environment will occupy the same niche.) Anyway, the next time somebody asks you that question, don't laugh at them or ridicule them. That's simply a surefire way to shut down any learning opportunity. Instead, take it as a teaching moment, and share a bit of the excitement of this topic.
Answer_with_writing_sample: The argument that the existence of monkeys disproves the theory of evolution is a common misunderstanding of how evolution works. First, it's essential to clarify that evolution does not claim that humans evolved directly from modern monkeys. Instead, humans and monkeys share a common ancestor that lived millions of years ago. This ancestor diverged into different lineages, leading to the evolution of various species, including the primates we see today. Monkeys are not "failed" experiments in evolution; they are simply a branch on the evolutionary tree that has adapted to their environments in their own unique ways. Moreover, the theory of evolution is supported by a vast body of evidence, including fossil records, genetic similarities, and observed evolutionary processes in various species. For instance, we can see how certain traits develop over generations in response to environmental pressures. It's also worth noting that evolution is not a linear progression but rather a complex web of branching paths, where different species can evolve simultaneously from shared ancestors. Thus, the existence of monkeys does not contradict evolution; rather, it exemplifies the diversity of life that has arisen through evolutionary processes. In essence, the argument against evolution based on the existence of monkeys reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of the theory itself, which is far more nuanced and supported by extensive scientific research.

Question: Can people not understand that the vast majority of religious people accept evolution and all science? That only a small fringe in a few countries with inferior educational systems talk creationist or other science denialist nonsense?
Old_Answer: No, I don't think you can say that "the vast majority of religious people accept evolution" or that the problem is confined to just "a small fringe in a few countries". Luckily, there’s polling data on this, so let’s take a look. To start off, since it's easiest to find detailed polling data on this for the U.S., here's the data for the U.S. broken down by religion: ABOVE: Pew Results about Human Evolution and Religion from 2018 Poll SOURCE: Data from Religious Landscape Study, Graph redrawn by me Buddhists, Hindus, and Jews all have very high levels of acceptance of evolution – around 80% or higher. That’s probably high enough to consider it a 'vast majority'. But among Christians, Catholics are the group with the most widespread acceptance of evolution, and they're only at 65%, or just under 2/3 acceptance. That's not exactly overwhelming. Evangelical Protestant's and Jehovah's Witnesses are downright hostile towards evolution, with majorities actually supporting creationism. I was able to find similar data for the UK and Canada broken down by religious vs. non-religious: ABOVE: YouGov Results about Human Evolution and Religion from 2017 Poll SOURCE: Data from ScienceReligionSpectrum.org - Resources and Information, Graph redrawn by me Among the religious/spiritual folks in the UK, only 63% supported evolution, while in Canada it was only 54%. Granted, those are majorities, but not vast majorities. For most other countries and regions, I couldn't find quite as detailed of data. It either listed only acceptance rates, or else didn't break things down by religion. At any rate, here are a few of those: ABOVE: Latin American Views on Evolution by Relgion from 2014 Report SOURCE: Pew Forum ABOVE: Views on Evolution in Eastern Europe from 2017 Report SOURCE: Pew Forum, slightly modified by me ABOVE: Worldwide Views on Evolution from 2011 Report SOURCE: Data from Ipsos, Graph by me There are very few countries or regions that I would characterize as having the "vast majority" supporting evolution. And especially when you look at that last graph, Europe overall only has a slim majority of folks supporting evolution – and it's the highest of any region! Most regions only have minority support of evolution (even if it is a plurality in most of them). So no, I don't think you can say that "the vast majority of religious people accept evolution", or that "only a small fringe in a few countries with inferior educational systems" support creationism. Creationism is a much bigger problem than your question acknowledges.

Question: If you are an atheist, do you like Sam Harris? What about Richard Dawkins?
Old_Answer: Out of those two, I only ever paid much attention to Richard Dawkins, so I'll limit my comments to him. He's... okay. Back around 20 years ago when I first started on my path to atheism, Dawkins was one of the leading voices for atheism and science (not the same thing, but so-called 'New Atheism' did/does rely heavily on science). He seemed to be a pretty sensible guy. He was involved in some good public campaigns for atheism (e.g. the Atheist Bus Campaign), and some more questionable ones (e.g. the Brights movement). But by and large, he was a reasonable voice for godlessness. If he was a 'militant' atheist, then there wasn't that much actual militancy within atheism. I finally purchased and read The God Delusion after I was already an atheist (I was too ashamed to be seen buying it at my local bookstore when I was still struggling with religion). It was a decent book that introduced me to things I'd never thought of before, though I haven't gone back to read it recently to see how well it holds up. The next book of his that I read was The Greatest Show on Earth, devoted to explaining the evidence for evolution. But I felt like he spent too much of that book harping on creationism, rather than focusing on the far more interesting topic of evolution itself. I read two other books on evidence for evolution around that same time, Jerry Coyne's Why Evolution Is True, and Donald Prothero's Evolution: What the Fossils Say and Why it Matters, and I recommend both of those books head and shoulders above Dawkins' Greatest Show on Earth. They both found a much better balance of dealing with creationism without it becoming distracting. After that, I read The Magic of Reality. This one was marketed to readers of all ages as a sort of broad science lesson on several topics, from 'Who was the first person' to rainbows to earthquakes. But once again, he harped so much on religion that it felt a bit like The God Delusion for Kids. His axe to grind against religion caused him to miss an opportunity to focus on the science. After that, I'm not sure if I drifted away from following him as closely, or if he himself drifted out of the public eye, but I didn't pay as much attention to him in the following years. I did notice from time to time that he seemed to stick his foot in his mouth on Twitter (I'm honestly not sure if he's even still active on 'X'). But given his age and the way plenty of old people don't keep up with shifting societal norms, while that might be a tad disappointing, it's not shocking (I cringed plenty of times listening to my own older relatives complaining about the changing times). Anyway, I found Dawkins to be a useful voice for atheism and science a couple decades ago when I first became an atheist and when I got involved in the Skeptical movement. After that, I found that he allowed his obsession with religion to mar what could otherwise have been better books. And then after that, I just kind of drifted away from following him, so I can't say too much about his present day activities.
Answer_with_writing_sample: As an atheist, I find both Sam Harris and Richard Dawkins to be compelling figures in the realm of secular thought, though my appreciation for them varies. On the other hand, Dawkins, particularly known for "The God Delusion," takes a more confrontational stance against religion, which can be both invigorating and polarizing. Ultimately, I think it's essential to engage with their ideas critically, appreciating the insights they offer while also acknowledging the limitations of their perspectives. In a world where religion often dominates discourse, having voices like Harris and Dawkins can help foster a more rational and evidence-based conversation about belief and morality.

Old_Answer: There's a big difference between the capital G God of the Bible, and a more generic lower case g god or higher power. The generic higher power is more difficult to 'disprove', and it's in this sense that many atheists admit there's still a small possibility of a god existing. But the capital G God of the Bible? Well, we've got the Bible itself to look at, along with archaeology. I've written about such things many times on Quora, and it would be easy to turn this into a Gish Gallop. In fact, I've already written such a 'Gish Gallop' type answer, which itself includes many links to other answers and articles: The introduction to that question is as good a summary as any: In short, the Bible seems exactly like the type of collection of stories that would develop organically over generations within a bronze age to iron age culture, and nothing at all like an inerrant work inspired by an actual God. There are all types of indications and clues within the Bible itself of how it developed over the generations, including the people’s changing concept of Yahweh. The early parts in Genesis seem like just-so stories that obviously don't match history on a literal level, and later parts like Exodus and the conquest of the Holy Land don't match archaeological evidence. And on top of all that, there are some stories that are just absurd at face value. To list just one example here, I'll go with the Kuntillet Ajrud inscriptions*. The Kuntillet Ajrud archaeological site dates to some time around the 8th century, B.C. It was most likely "an Israelite state-sponsored enterprise" (source: The Inscriptions of Kuntillet ‛Ajrud Through the Lens of Historical Research). Among the findings there are inscriptions and drawings mentioning El, Yahweh, Ba'al, and Yahweh's wife, Asherah. For example, one of these inscriptions (on Pithos A) includes: I have blessed you by YHWH of Samaria and to [his†] Asherata. While another (on Pithos B) includes: I have blessed you by YHWH of Teman and [his†] Asherata. ABOVE: A projection drawing of Pithos A, which includes the wording, "I have blessed you by YHWH of Samaria and to [his†] Asherata." SOURCE: https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Projection-drawing-of-Pithos-A-Meshel-et-al-2012-87-Fig-524-147-Fig-65-tags_fig1_318275592 So, right off the bat, we have a depiction of Yahweh that predates the composition of much of the the Bible‡, and shows the belief that he had a wife. (And note that these weren't the only two such inscriptions from the site.) This shows that the precursor to monotheistic Judaism was a polytheistic religion, where Yahweh wasn't the only god or goddess. It's also significant that there were separate mentions of a Yahweh of Samaria and a Yahweh of Teman. At the very least, these types of localized centers of worship contradict the Biblical narrative that the worship of Yahweh had been centralized to the Temple of Jerusalem by that point. But, according to that paper I already linked to, the author believes these different Yahwehs actually represent different regional deities with "distinct cultic vessels, rituals and ceremonies". The Yahweh of Samaria was only concerned with Samaria, while the Yahweh of Teman was concerned only with Teman. And further, a certain amount of the Deuteronomistic influence§ in the Bible was trying to bring these disparate religions and customs together into a unified religion for all of Israel and Judah. As one more quick note, another inscription from the site contains what may be a version of the story of Moses and the Exodus, but, according to that same paper, with "marked differences compared to the canonical biblical story, confirming the assumption of scholars that biblical traditions developed gradually over many years." So, from the archaeological findings at Kuntillet Ajrud, we have evidence showing one of the steps in the development of Yahweh, as a local deity with a goddess for a wife, before he developed into the monotheistic God of all creation that most people are familiar with, now. We also have details showing that the Biblical narrative isn't completely trustworthy, since worship of Yahweh hadn't yet been centralized to the Temple at Jerusalem like the story claims. And as I said, that's just from one archaeological site. That other answer that I already linked to provides many, many more examples. Question: If you throw an object up into the air in a moving car, why doesn't it go flying backwards?
Old_Answer: This gets to the heart of Newton's Laws of Motion. Although many of us engineers and other technical folks take them for granted, now, they really did go against people's common sense intuition. Living in an environment like we do, where friction is ever-present, many people intuitively feel that a force must be continuously applied to an object for it to continue moving. Newton's insight can be summed up in his famous first law (copied here from Wikipedia’s paraphrase): A body remains at rest, or in motion at a constant speed in a straight line, except insofar as it is acted upon by a force. The reason why objects in our everyday lives always slow down is because they're always subjected to external forces that slow them down, namely friction and air resistance. If it wasn't for those external forces, once you started an object in motion, it would continue moving forever, or at least until some other force acted upon it. So, when you're riding along in a car, the car, you, and any other objects in the car are all moving along at some speed. Let's just say 60 mph for the sake of argument. So, if you throw an object up inside the car, what force is going to slow it down? All the air in the car is traveling along with you at that same 60 mph, so there won't be any drag. Nothing else is touching the object to impart friction. So there isn't any force in the horizontal direction to slow the object down, and it'll continue right along at that 60 mph. Now, in the vertical direction, you did throw the object up to begin with, which gave it a starting force and corresponding vertical speed. And then the force of gravity will continuously pull it down, which will initially slow its upward speed, and eventually result in an ever increasing downward speed until you catch it again. Assuming this object is something hefty enough to ignore the small amount of air resistance (i.e. not a feather), after it leaves your hand, the only significant force would be gravity. So if we were to draw what's known as a free body diagram, it would look like this: So, with a force in only one direction, that's the only direction in which speed will change. Now, if we threw the object out the window instead of keeping it inside the car, that's a whole different story. Ignoring any wind, the air outside the car is essentially motionless. So as soon as the object hits that air, there will be air resistance. Now, the object will have at least two forces acting on it – the air resistance and the gravity. So now, the object will change speed in both the vertical and horizontal directions. Gravity will pull it downwards, while the air resistance will slow it down relative to the car. So from your perspective in the car, it will go flying backwards. But, just to point out one more thing, consider it from the point of view of somebody standing by the side of the road watching you. When you threw the object out the window, they wouldn't see it go flying backwards. They would see you, the car, and the object all initially at 60 mph. Then, the object would slow down while you and the car kept on going at 60 mph. You'd all be moving forward, it's just that you and the car would be going faster than the object. The figure below is about dropping a bomb, but it shows basically the same thing: ABOVE: Notice the difference between the ‘Vacuum Trajectory’ (with no drag) vs. the ‘Actual Trajectory’ (with drag) SOURCE: CHAPTER-23-D Basically, the reason an object tossed in a car doesn't go flying backwards is because it was already moving at the same speed as you and the car, and there's no force to change that.
Answer_with_writing_sample: When you throw an object up into the air while in a moving car, it doesn't fly backwards due to the principles of inertia and relative motion. According to Newton's First Law of Motion, an object in motion will remain in motion unless acted upon by an external force. When you toss the object upwards, it retains the forward velocity of the car at the moment of release. So, while the car is moving forward, the object is also moving forward at the same speed. To an observer inside the car, it appears to go straight up and then come straight down, but to someone outside the car, the object follows a parabolic trajectory, moving forward as it rises and falls. This is why it doesn't seem to fly backwards; it's simply maintaining the same horizontal speed as the car. The only time it would appear to go backwards is if the car suddenly decelerates or stops, which would create a relative motion effect where the object would continue moving forward due to its inertia while the car slows down. In essence, the object behaves according to the laws of physics, and its motion is influenced by the speed of the car at the moment of release, leading to the intuitive observation that it doesn't fly backwards but rather follows a predictable path influenced by both gravity and the car's motion.

However, under normal circumstances, the object's forward motion remains consistent with the car's speed, making it seem as though it simply goes up and down rather than flying backward. This fascinating interplay of forces and motion is a great example of how our everyday experiences are governed by the laws of physics, often in ways that aren't immediately obvious.

Question: How has technology changed our lives?
Old_Answer: Technology essentially made our species possible. It's so ingrained into human existence that we barely even think about the most basic forms of technology, but we wouldn't be here without it. One of the most basic technologies, controlled use of fire, goes back at least around 1 million years. That predates Homo sapiens. It was probably Homo erectus that first developed that technology. Purposely shaped stone tools go back even further – 3.3 million years. That's before our ancestors had even evolved into the Homo genus. Those tools were probably made by something like Australopithecus afarensis or Kenyanthropus platyops. ABOVE SOURCE: Oldest stone tools pre-date earliest humans If you look at humans compared to a lot of other animals, while we're not as physically pathetic as some hyperbolic documentaries try to make us out to be, we're still on the slow, weak side when un-armed. But those ancient technologies that our ancestors developed allowed them to hunt, defend themselves, cook food, etc. That in turn allowed our ancestors to develop large, calorie hungry brains, while compensating with smaller muscles that didn't need as much nutrition as some of our bulkier cousins (I'm looking at you, gorillas, with your 5 to 10k calorie per day food requirements – The Influence of Seasonal Frugivory on Nutrient and Energy Intake in Wild Western Gorillas). Without that level of already existing technology in our pre-human ancestors, our own evolution just wouldn't have happened. Question: Does it bother atheists that people believe in God?
Old_Answer: It does bother me that people believe in gods, but the extent to which it bothers me depends very much on the specifics of how the person acts. Look, most of my friends are Christians. And for the most part, we only discuss religion a bit, and have a live and let live attitude. As long as people are reasonable and tolerant, religion isn't the type of thing that gets me up in arms. But even then, it still bothers me some. I mean, I think back to when I was still a Christian, and all the cognitive dissonance I experienced, the fear of Hell (especially for others besides myself), the Catholic guilt, the wrestling with secular ethics vs. Biblical rules, etc. It may have taken me a few years to get to this point, but I'm happier now as an atheist than I was as a Christian, and I'd like for others to have that. But, I also don't want to be that guy that's always arguing and being pushy about beliefs. So here's a list of examples stepping through different types of believers and how I feel about them. Type of Believer: Tolerant believer who keeps their religion private and doesn't impose on others My Feelings: This bothers me on the same level as people who believe in urban legends, or who root for different sports teams from me. They're wrong about the nature of reality, and I would like to help them see the world more clearly, and recognize that the Steelers are the one true... sorry - wrong topic Level of Opposition: Good natured discussions over beer (though I hardly ever bring it up, waiting for others to broach the subject) Type of Believer: Somewhat tolerant believer, but who lets their religious beliefs influence the way they vote (particularly if they vote against women's rights or LGBT rights, or think global warming can't be real because God wouldn't let it happen) My Feelings: Well, now your religious beliefs aren't as private anymore, since they're having real world effects. So, now I do feel more justified in trying to get you to change your mind. Level of Opposition: More heated discussions over beer, Possible end of friendship depending on how they treat individuals Type of Believer: Door to door proselytizers My Feelings: Hoo boy. I love debate, and I have strong opinions on religion, and you actually came to my house with the purpose of talking about religion, so here we go. Level of Opposition: Debate for as long as they're willing to stay at my house Type of Believer: Parents who withhold real medical treatment from children in favor of faith healing My Feelings: I don't personally know anyone like this, but I know they're out there. The case of Makayla Sault was a heartbreaking, recent example. Children shouldn't have to suffer or die for the religious beliefs of their parents. Level of Opposition: Push for laws to outlaw this type of child abuse Type of Believer: Intolerant believer, who lets their religious beliefs influence the way they vote and how they treat individuals (particularly women, the LGBT community, and people outside their faith) My Feelings: Yeah, now they're definitely into the strong negative effects of religion, and I don't just feel justified to try to change their minds, but see it as a moral duty to society. Level of Opposition: Strong debate, definitely not going to be friends Type of Believer: Preachers/Leaders of Creationist/Evangelical/Fundamentalist Groups My Feelings: You're not just misleading yourself, but misleading all the people who follow you. And these brands of religion are usually the more close-minded branches that lead to negative effects, so I'm definitely going to speak up. Level of Opposition: Pointed blog entries and Quora answers Type of Believer: Intolerant Religious Politicians My Feelings: We have a First Amendment for a reason. Government and religion aren't supposed to be intertwined. It really, really bothers me when politicians pass religiously based laws, or give preferential treatment to certain religious institutions. Level of Opposition: Pointed blog entries and Quora answers, Vote for opponent So, that's how I feel about it. We live in a free, multicultural society, where people have the right to believe anything they want. As long as religious people are tolerant of others and don't use religion as a reason to discriminate or make bad decisions, the most they'll have to fear from me is talking about religion over a beer every once in a while. However, if a person's religious beliefs are having harmful, real-world consequences, then I'm going to speak up.
